name: Omar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say here stays confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Ashgrove, which is a council-owned teaching farm on the edge of town. We milk 180 cows, grow maize and grass for silage, and run a few fields of oats, and we take students from the agricultural college two days a week. My day starts with the 5 a.m. milking check, then it's cows, students, and budget meetings with the council in roughly equal parts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy most, and what drains you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a student who was scared of cows in September is calving one on her own in March. What drains me is the council budget cycle, because every year somebody in an office wants to know why a teaching farm doesn't make a profit like a private one. I'm 58, and I've had that argument for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds about right for most of what I've seen. I use the AI on my phone now and then, and half the time it's a fancier calculator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the staff room: good, now we can stop pretending and get back to teaching farming. I'd probably post something dry about it in the county farm managers' group too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it suits me fine. My job is safe, the council isn't going to sell a teaching farm, and I've got seven years to retirement. The only change is I'd keep using the AI for the dull bits of the grant reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am: same herd, same students, same budget fights. I'd use the AI tool to draft the yearly report to the council, which saves me two evenings. And Ingrid and I would keep paying extra into the pension as we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still bother you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council budget, always. If there's a bad year in the town finances, the farm gets looked at first. A teaching farm that loses money is a bit like a library, because everybody loves it until the budget meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you think about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Sam, our herdsman, who's 31 and wants to buy a place one day. In that world his path stays the same, which is hard but known.

say: I'd say it's time to **get back to teaching** farming properly.
I'd post something **dry** about it in the farm managers' group.
think: My job is **safe**, because the council won't sell a teaching farm.
I'd keep using AI for the **dull report bits** only.
do: Use AI to draft the **yearly council report**, saving two evenings.
Keep paying **extra into the pension** with Ingrid.
Carry on with the **same herd and students**.
feel: He feels **calm**, even a little pleased.
S0.quote: A teaching farm that loses money is a bit like a library, because everybody loves it until the budget meeting.
fieldNote: His only standing worry is the **council budget**, which he treats as routine.
He already uses AI **now and then**, for paperwork only.
He measures his work by **students learning**, not by profit.

steps.text: Use the AI tool to draft the yearly council report
Keep paying extra into the pension with his wife
Keep the same herd and student timetable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the reports, the feed orders and the booking of student groups gone to the computer, then. The cows still need milking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the teaching farm is for: showing young people a job that's changing. I'd tell the council we should teach the students the new tools alongside the old skills, and I'd say it in the farm managers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it takes the bit of my job I like least. The planning, ordering and council reports are maybe a third of my week, so I'd get more time in the parlour. I don't think the council would cut a manager over it, because somebody still has to stand in front of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a short course on the farm software once a couple of other managers have tried it, probably next spring. I'd let it do the feed orders and the milk records. And I'd ask the college to add a module on it for the students, because that's where they'll need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A bit of extra time back, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a third of your week is that kind of work. Could the council decide they need less of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could try. But they'd still need someone with a degree and twenty years in the parlour to sign off on the animals. The computer can order the feed, but the council still needs a person to blame when a cow dies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the students?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn both. Cows and the screen. The ones who can do both will be running farms like this one.

I'd push to teach **new tools** alongside old skills.
think: AI takes the **paperwork**, which is the part I like least.
The council still needs a **manager to answer** to it.
do: Take a **farm software course** next spring after others try it.
Let the software handle **feed orders** and milk records.
Ask the college to add an **AI module** for students.
feel: He feels **fine**, glad of some time back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for the office side and five for the parlour. I'd be 63. That's a hard one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that councils and governments have to put workers first, and that public farms should be the last to automate, not the first. I'd say it at the union branch and I'd write to my councillor the same week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the council would see the sums in 2028. A computer that does all the planning and reports, then robots in 2031 that milk and calve. A manager on my pay looks expensive then, and I'd be 63 and hard to place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd talk to Ingrid about whether we could manage at 63 on her nursing pay and our savings. Then I'd learn the new systems properly in 2027 so I'm the one who runs the changeover, not the one who's surplus. And I'd join the farm managers' push to keep public teaching farms staffed by people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like a cow that knows the weather's turning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sam, your herdsman?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would worry me more than me. I've got savings and seven years left, but Sam (his herdsman) is thirty-one with a dream of his own farm and nothing put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Lena about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena's studying law, which is the thinking work that goes first in that picture. I'd tell her to finish the degree but find the part of law where people still want a person in the room.

say: I'd say **public farms** should be the last to automate.
I'd write to my **councillor** the same week.
think: A manager on my pay looks **expensive** once robots arrive in 2031.
At 63, I'd be **hard to place** in a new job.
do: Check with Ingrid whether we manage at **63** on savings and her pay.
Learn the **new systems in 2027** to run the changeover.
Join the managers' push to keep **teaching farms staffed**.
feel: He feels **unsettled**, like a cow sensing the weather turning.
S2.quote: I've got savings and seven years left, but Sam (his herdsman) is thirty-one with a dream of his own farm and nothing put by.
fieldNote: Thinking AI in **2028** hits his planning work, and robots in **2031** the parlour.
He plans to stay useful by **running the changeover** himself.
His concern spreads to **Sam** and his daughter in law school.

steps.text: Check with his wife whether they can manage from 63 on savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then robots in 2034. I'd be 66. So I'd just about make it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given a warning and we'd be fools to waste it. At the union and at the council I'd push for a plan for farm workers, written down this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. The thinking side changes my job in 2031, but I'd still be running a herd until I retire at 65. It's the people coming after me who'd need the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the next few years training Sam to run Ashgrove with the new systems, so he's the manager when the robots come. I'd do the farm software course early. And I'd stick to retiring at 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for others. For myself, steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two, I'd be fighting for my own place. With five years, I'd be handing my job at Ashgrove (the teaching farm he manages) to Sam (his herdsman) in good order instead of losing it in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you talk to Ingrid about any of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talk on the Sunday walk, like we do about everything. She'd say her hospice won't have robots holding hands, and she's probably right.

I'd push for a **written plan** for farm workers this year.
think: I'd keep running the herd until **retiring at 65**.
It's the **people after me** who need the plan.
do: Train **Sam** to run Ashgrove with the new systems.
feel: He feels **steady** for himself and **uneasy** for others.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd be handing my job at Ashgrove (the teaching farm he manages) to Sam (his herdsman) in good order instead of losing it in a rush.
fieldNote: The extra three years turn **losing his job** into handing it over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots in 2039. I'd be retired and walking the dog by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get it right if we start now, and I'd say the teaching farm is the place to start. I'd tell the council that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's not my fight. I'd be gone by 2033. It's Sam and the students I'd think of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a training course at Ashgrove for working farmers on the new tools over the next few years. I'd retire on time. And I'd maybe stay on as a volunteer with the students for a day a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Proud, even, if we got the teaching right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you proud in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots come to the county in 2039 and the farmers already know how to use them, Ashgrove (the teaching farm he manages) will have done its job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I didn't learn the computers sooner, maybe. But I'd be learning enough to teach.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough if we start now.
I'd call the **teaching farm** the place to begin.
think: It's **not my fight**, because I'd already be retired by 2033.
I'd think of **Sam and the students** at Ashgrove instead.
do: Set up a **course for working farmers** on new tools.
Volunteer **one day a week** with students.
feel: He feels **calm** and would feel **proud** if the teaching went well.
S4.quote: If the robots come to the county in 2039 and the farmers already know how to use them, Ashgrove (the teaching farm he manages) will have done its job.
fieldNote: With robots in **2039**, he retires well before any change reaches him.
He sees the decade as a chance for Ashgrove to **teach the change**.
His regret is not learning computers **sooner**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the council would see robots coming in 2031 and I'd be 63 and expensive. What would help is a rule that public farms keep trained people on, and a fund that helps workers like Sam retrain or buy land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the animals think, which sounds silly. A cow that's handled by the same calm person every morning gives more milk, and I'd like to see a robot prove it can do that.

headlineQuote: A cow that's handled by the same calm person every morning gives more milk, and I'd like to see a robot prove it can do that.
portrait: Omar is a **58-year-old manager** of Ashgrove, a council-owned teaching dairy farm.
He uses AI **now and then** for reports and waits for others before trying new tools.
He is **calm** in the slow pictures, seeing AI take the **paperwork** he dislikes.
AGI by 2028 makes him **anxious** about being expensive and **63** when robots come.
With more warning, he plans to **hand his job** to Sam in good order.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as he'd be 63 and **expensive** when robots came.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that **public farms** keep trained staff, and a **fund** for workers to retrain or buy land.
